title: Volcker Disinflation Turn
text: With inflation falling, the Fed moved away from strict reserve targeting. Short-term interest rates began a broad decline from their early-1980s highs.

title: 1984 Tightening Peak
text: A powerful economic recovery, rapid money growth, heavy borrowing, and concern that inflation could return kept monetary policy restrictive. The federal funds rate climbed above 11%, while mortgage rates exceeded 14%. Rates began falling later in 1984 as economic growth moderated.

title: Inflation Pressures Build
text: A falling dollar, higher import and energy prices, and worsening inflation expectations increased pressure on the Fed to act. The Fed would tighten policy shortly afterward, pushing the funds rate to 6.58% in May and 6.75% in June.

title: Black Monday
text: After the October 19 stock-market crash, the Fed supplied liquidity to the financial system and allowed interest rates to decline.

title: 1989 Tightening Peak
text: After tightening policy through 1988 and early 1989 to restrain inflation, the Fed held the funds rate near 9.75%. By late spring, employment, consumer spending, housing, and money growth were weakening, prompting a shift toward rate cuts beginning in mid-1989.

title: Recession Easing Begins
text: The Fed lowered its target to 8.00% as the economy entered recession. Rate cuts continued through 1992.

title: Rate Reaches 3 Percent
text: The final cut of the 1990–1992 easing cycle brought the federal funds target down to 3.00%.

title: Aggressive Tightening Begins
text: The Fed raised its target from 3.00% to 3.25%, beginning a tightening cycle that eventually brought the rate to 6.00%.

title: Soft-Landing Cut
text: After the aggressive 1994 tightening cycle, the Fed lowered the target to 5.75% as inflation pressures eased.

title: Russia and LTCM Crisis
text: Following Russia’s default and instability surrounding Long-Term Capital Management, the Fed began three rapid cuts that lowered the target to 4.75%.

title: Dot-Com Easing Begins
text: Two January cuts lowered the target from 6.50% to 5.50%. The recession and September 11 attacks led to additional cuts during 2001.

title: Post-Dot-Com Low
text: The Fed reduced the target to 1.00% amid a weak recovery and concerns about inflation becoming too low.

title: Pre-Crisis Peak
text: The seventeenth consecutive quarter-point increase raised the target to 5.25%, where it remained until September 2007.

title: Financial-Crisis Cuts Begin
text: As housing and credit-market problems intensified, the Fed cut the target by half a percentage point to 4.75%.

title: Zero Lower Bound
text: With the financial crisis worsening, the Fed established a 0%–0.25% target range and increasingly relied on unconventional policies such as quantitative easing.

title: Liftoff From Zero
text: The Fed raised the target range to 0.25%–0.50%, its first increase since 2006 and the beginning of policy normalization.

title: Mid-Cycle Adjustment
text: The Fed lowered the range to 2.00%–2.25%, its first cut since 2008, amid trade uncertainty and slowing global growth.

title: Pandemic Emergency Cuts
text: Two emergency cuts totaling 1.50 percentage points returned the target range to 0%–0.25% as the COVID-19 crisis struck the economy.

title: Inflation Fight Begins
text: The Fed raised the range to 0.25%–0.50%, beginning an unusually rapid tightening cycle intended to control inflation.

title: Tightening Cycle Peak
text: The final quarter-point increase brought the target range to 5.25%–5.50%, its highest level since 2001.

title: Easing Cycle Begins
text: With inflation moderating and employment risks increasing, the Fed cut the target range by half a percentage point to 4.75%–5.00%.

title: Fed Reverses Course
text: After three cuts in late 2025 lowered the range to 3.50%–3.75%, the Fed raised it by a quarter point to 3.75%–4.00% because inflation remained elevated.
